title: The teacher
hook: in Tibetan practice the teacher is central; students are told to check a teacher for years first

segments.voice: Yesterday: four thoughts that turn the mind, and your line, turn the mind. When an old groove pulled at you, did you pause and choose? Day three hundred nine.

A contractor gets his references checked. A dentist gets her reviews read. And yet people sometimes hand their whole inner life, their time, their money, their trust, to a charismatic stranger after one inspiring weekend. Tibetan Buddhism puts the teacher at the center of the path. And the same tradition tells students, in writing: slow down. Check first. Some texts say to take years. Today: the lama, and how to look at one.
screen: `REFERENCES FOR A CONTRACTOR.` → `ONE WEEKEND, A WHOLE LIFE.` → `SLOW DOWN. CHECK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Lama is the Tibetan word for the Sanskrit guru. Guru literally means heavy: someone of weight, whose words land. Tibetans give lama their own warm explanations too; a common one says it means none higher. Why is the teacher so central here? Because many Vajrayana practices are passed from person to person. A teacher reads the text aloud so the student receives it, gives permission for a practice, and shows how it's done, the way a music teacher shows you how to hold the bow. You can read about the violin forever. At some point, someone has to hear you play. But the same tradition insists on caution. A text called the Fifty Verses on the Guru tells teacher and student to examine each other first, and Tibetan teachers often say this can take as long as twelve years. The Dalai Lama has said many times that students should scrutinize a teacher carefully, and that no one should follow an instruction that goes against the teaching or against basic ethics. Classic lists describe a good teacher as disciplined, calm, learned, loving, and tireless in teaching. And there are warning signs anyone can see: pressure, secrecy, money that's never explained, being cut off from friends, behavior that breaks the very precepts being taught. Recent decades have shown why this matters: some communities have been hurt by teachers who abused their trust, and Tibetan teachers, the Dalai Lama among them, have said such harm should be made public. The heart of it is simple. Trust is given slowly, and it stays open to question. Check the teacher.
screen: `LAMA — GURU, ONE OF WEIGHT.` · `PASSED FROM PERSON TO PERSON.` · `EXAMINE EACH OTHER, FOR YEARS.` · `SIGNS OF A GOOD TEACHER, AND WARNINGS.` · then, large: `CHECK THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, think of anyone who has taught you something that mattered: a coach, a grandparent, a boss, a teacher in any field. What made them trustworthy? Maybe they admitted mistakes. Maybe they never asked for more than they gave. Silently name two or three of those qualities. Then let the list go, and sit with the breath, noticing that you, too, get to be careful about whom you trust. The bell holds the time.
Lama. The Tibetan word for guru, a teacher of weight: central to the path, and to be examined carefully first.
Your line: check the teacher. Today, write down the qualities you named, so you have them the next time someone asks for your trust. Day three hundred nine.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism students usually study with a lama who gives teachings, reading transmissions and empowerments; many teachers advise students to observe a teacher for a long time before committing to one.

match.prompt: match what the tradition says about teachers.

fork.setup: you've found an inspiring teacher. after a month, they ask you to keep the group's finances secret and to stop seeing old friends. what does the tradition itself advise?
options: slow down, keep checking, and step back if it breaks ethics.
fork.reveal: the tradition that makes the teacher central also says to examine a teacher carefully and not follow instructions against basic ethics.

original.note: Tibetan bla ma, translating Sanskrit guru; a common Tibetan explanation reads it as 'none higher'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lama is any Tibetan monk.
what it means: a teacher, central to the path, whom students are told to examine carefully first.
what a scholar hears: bla ma renders Sanskrit guru, 'heavy', and not every monk is a lama nor every lama a monk; many lamas are lay teachers, some married.

sources.ref: Fifty Verses on the Guru (Gurupancashika), on mutual examination
Gampopa, Jewel Ornament of Liberation, chapter on the spiritual friend (qualities of a teacher)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they would do, and drops the comparative 'the tradition that puts the teacher at the very center... is also the one' framing; the teacher-qualities list now follows the classical list Gampopa cites (disciplined, calm, learned, loving, tireless) instead of the modern 'honest about what they don't know'; 'many Tibetan teachers have said' narrowed to 'Tibetan teachers, the Dalai Lama among them'.

Confirm the Dalai Lama's public statements (around 2017-2018) that abuse by teachers should be made public, and that the qualities list matches Jewel Ornament of Liberation's chapter on the spiritual friend.
'Twelve years' of mutual examination is a common Tibetan teaching associated with the Fifty Verses on the Guru; the verse wording varies. Confirm.
The Dalai Lama's statements on scrutinizing teachers and refusing unethical instructions are paraphrased from many public talks: confirm framing.
The paragraph on abuse in some communities is deliberately general (no names). Keeper should confirm tone.
'None higher' is a popular gloss of bla ma, not a strict etymology: flagged as a Tibetan explanation.
